title: City Council Regular Meeting
overview: The Glendale City Council held a long public hearing on a Glendale Water & Power plan to raise water rates over five years, starting with a 53% revenue increase on January 1, 2027 and about 120% in total by 2031. Dozens of residents spoke, most against the increase or asking for more time. The council made no decision on the rates. It voted 5–0 to keep the hearing open and bring the item back on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, so written protests can still be turned in until the hearing closes at that meeting.

items.title: Glendale Water and Power, re: Public Hearing Regarding Proposed Water Rate Increases for Fiscal Years 2027–2031 and Resolution Establishing Water Rates and Charges; Motion Approving Glendale Water and Power Water System Cash Reserve Policy
items.headline: Council delays water rate decision one week after hours of mostly opposing testimony
items.summary: Glendale Water & Power (GWP) asked the council to approve five years of water rate increases: 53% more revenue in 2027, then 11%, 10%, 10% and 7%, which adds up to about 120% over five years. Staff said costs for imported water, electricity and equipment have risen much faster than rates since 2018. The money would pay for $100 million in pipe, tank, pump, fire-flow and water meter work, plus a $40 million bond that staff said depends on the January start date. Staff said a typical single-family home in the lowest zone would pay about $21–26 more per month, and homes in the highest zone about $71–86 more. Under Proposition 218, a state rule that lets property owners block a rate increase with written protests, the clerk reported 4,351 protests received, far short of the 22,738 needed. Most speakers opposed the increase or asked for a delay, while a few supported it. Council members raised a late letter from Forest Lawn about recycled water rates and an idea from Councilmember Gharpetian to rely on a flat meter charge instead. Staff said they needed time to study that idea and that it would require a new public notice.
items.whyItMatters: Water rates have not changed yet, but if the plan is approved at the November 17, 2026 meeting, most customers' water bills would rise sharply starting January 1, 2027, and residents can still submit written protests while the hearing stays open.

outcome.result: Approved 5–0 to keep the hearing open and continue the item one week, to November 17, 2026, without further public notice

transcript.speaker: speaker_1
transcript.text: All right. Um, Mr. Golanian, let's open this hearing at 7:38 PM and get started.

transcript.speaker: speaker_2
transcript.text: Yeah. Um, Mayor Kassakhian, member of City Council, in 2024, GWP engaged a consulting firm to conduct a comprehensive water financial plan and cost of service analysis, or COSA. transcript.speaker: speaker_2
transcript.text: On September 1st of this year, GWP staff presented the findings of that COSA and the proposed five-year water rate adjustments to the City Council, that on that evening authorized staff to proceed with the Proposition 218 notification and to schedule a public hearing to consider the proposed rate adjustments.

transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.speaker: speaker_2
transcript.text: We completely understand the financial concerns around the new water rate structure, and this evening's public hearing provides an opportunity for the City Council to receive public testimony, consider written protests submitted pursuant to, uh, Prop 218, and determine whether to adopt the proposed water rate adjustments.

transcript.speaker: speaker_2

transcript.speaker: speaker_3

And so we will talk a little bit about the why. Uh, we will also talk through some investments, uh, infrastructure projects that we'll be invested in, as well as, um, uh, some examples, as referenced by Mr.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, a- and so this really has been a very comprehensive, now nearly two-year process, uh, beginning with the Water Master Plan, uh, back in December of 2024, uh, in which we assessed the conditions of our water system. transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Following your council's authorization in September of 2026, um, is when we began the Proposition, uh, 218 notification process in which we facilitated four community meetings just last month, uh, which were very well attended, and we'll talk a little bit more about that later on in the presentation. transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, and so as always, I'd like to start with some background into our water supply and our water infrastructure. Uh, we deliver about twenty million gallons of water every single day. That's about 7.3 billion gallons per year, majority of which is imported from outside of our immediate region, right? We import water from two main sources, uh, the Colorado River as well as the State Water Project in Northern California through our partnership with Metropolitan Water District.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, again, that is about 60 to 70% of our water supply. Uh, the remaining 38% is comprised of local groundwater, uh, and to a smaller extent, recycled water to the tune of about 5%. Uh, and we use our recycled water solely, uh, for irrigation. And so we have about four sections that work together to ensure that, uh, safe, high quality water makes it to every single home and business in Glendale.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: That includes our water treatment section, right? We have two treatment facilities, one potable water and one for recycled water, which we co-own, uh, with the City of Los Angeles. Uh, but they essentially treat our water to ensure that it meets or exceeds all state or federal regulations. We also have our distribution section, and they oversee everything from the moment that water leaves the treatment facility to when it makes it to its destination at the customer's meter, uh, and everything in between, right?

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: That includes about well over four hundred miles of pipe infrastructure. Uh, that includes about thirty-six thousand customer meters. That includes about thirty pump stations and an equal number of tanks and reservoirs, and that includes well over thirty-two hundred fire hydrants. At any given moment within our distribution system, we have to ensure that that water is safe.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, as such, we have our water quality section, uh, and they collect samples of about eighty thousand samples every single year, which is tested, uh, by a third-party vendor, again, to ensure that we are meeting all state and federal drinking water regulations. Uh, and last but certainly not least is our engineering team, uh, and they are responsible for overseeing the implementation of both our capital, uh, and operational projects.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so for every single drop that we deliver, you know, behind that drop is, um, a dedicated team, uh, a very complex operation, bo-both, uh, regionally as well as locally here, um, a-and really a, a vast network of infrastructure, majority of which has aged beyond its useful life. And that was really the impetus for the commencement of the Water Master Plan almost two years ago.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so, uh, historical context here, the last time we completed a COSA was back in twenty eighteen, so about eight years ago. The table at the top here shows the corresponding rate increases from, from that COSA. And so that's about seven and a half percent, um, rate increase in the past eight years, well below inflation, which was nearly thirty percent in the same timeframe.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: In addition to that, the, you know, since twenty eighteen, the cost of providing water has significantly increased, right? Just to name a few, uh, the cost of imported water, which accounts for nearly forty percent of our O&M, operations and maintenance budget, that has inclu- that has increased by approximately forty-five percent, right? Electricity costs, uh, which is critical for us to be able to move water, pump water to higher elevation zones within our system, that cost has increased by well over fifty percent.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Other operational i- uh, items, our hydrants, our valves, pipe infrastructure, those costs continue to increase, some well over a hundred and thirty percent. And so simply put, cost has significantly outpaced revenues and, quite frankly, our ability to maintain the water system, uh, in the way that it needs to be maintained.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, and, and so with these rate increases, um, you know, we're proposing to invest a hundred million dollars into our infrastructure over the course of the next five years. And you can see the various categories or buckets, um, of projects in which we will be investing in. Um, pipe infrastructure, that will account for about thirty percent or thirty million dollars, uh, in our total proposed expenditures.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, a-and, you know, another reoccurring concern that we've heard throughout these, uh, process is, you know, whether replacing just two miles of pipe, uh, will really make a meaningful difference, um, because that is how much we are anticipated to replace on an annual basis over the next five years. Um, you know, two miles translates to about ten miles over the five-year period.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And now, while that may seem modest relative to our four hundred mile distribution system, uh, it's important to note that we're not just replacing these pipes at random, right? We are prioritizing the most vulnerable, uh, pipe infrastructure where the likelihood and the, uh, consequences of failure are greatest. And so, you know, we've seen the consequences of these failures in surrounding communities.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Um, they cause-- as mentioned by the speaker earlier, they cause significant disruption in water service, um, property damage, um, a-and they compromise public health and safety. Uh, and so the question really isn't whether replacing two miles will make-- will fix all of our pipe problems, because that is not the intent, but rather whether replacing ten miles over five years will help drive down the risk of these catastrophic failures.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And again, that is the intent of our pipe replacement program. And, you know, in the future, um, a-as resources become available, we certainly endeavor to increase the mileage of pipe that we replace. Uh, however, as it stands today, uh, we do have competing priorities. We have a finite amount of resources, and we want to remain sensitive to the potential cost impacts, right?

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: We want to moderate the potential cost increases, uh, to our customers. Moving on, we also will be investing about ten million dollars into improving our fire protection capabilities, right? Our Water Master Plan identified several areas where, um, we lack adequate water pressure. Um, we lack adequate flow to be able to ensure fire standards.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Um, you know, and again, this is not uncommon when you have a water system that's well over a hundred years old, uh, and you have fire codes that were widely established in the seventies and eighties. I think the difference is that we acknowledge, uh, these deficien-deficiencies, and we're taking the necessary step to bring them up to standard. Forty-two million dollars will go into replacing our facilities, right?

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: So this is our tanks, this is our reservoirs. Uh, and this also includes installing permanent generators at critical pump stations. Uh, in the event of a power outage, we want to continue to ensure water reliability. Uh, again, the majority of our, uh, pumps-- all of our pumps actually run on electricity.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so we're also investing in our aging water meters, uh, to be able to improve our billing accuracy. Uh, and the total project cost for that project is twenty-six million dollars, with eleven million dollars already accounted for, uh, last fiscal year, twenty-six, and the remaining fifteen million dollars is included in fiscal year twenty-seven budget as part of, uh, this COSA.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, and then we are also looking at, um, opportunities to invest in local water supplies to be able to develop, uh, locally produced water here in Glendale. Um, uh, we all recognize the significant challenges we're facing with imported water. They're becoming less economical. They're becoming less sustainable. And so to the extent that we can have, um, this drought-proof, locally sourced water here in Glendale, um, we essentially hold our own power, and that is the intent of this study: to identify opportunities to be able to undertake that.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so this table outlines the categories of projects to be completed over the next five years. Uh, again, that is a total five-year investment of $100 million. And so how does that compare to historical capital spending? Right. So in the past five years, in fiscal years '22 to '26, we've averaged close to about $5 million in capital expenditures.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: We are proposing to quadruple that to an average of $20 million per year, right? And this represents a significant shift from a reactive approach to maintaining our infrastructure to a more proactive, more systematic, uh, approach to our infrastructure replacement program. A-and this is the level or the pace of investment that we need in order to be able to catch up, uh, with our infrastructure.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so this shows our total five-year expenditure plan. Uh, it includes all of our O&M, our capital outlay. Uh, it includes our debt service, both existing and proposed. Uh, and our largest expenses include, uh, purchasing imported water. As mentioned, that is a significant cost, uh, about $145 million, uh, planned over the next five years.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, we also have our day-to-day operations, right? This includes contractual services. Uh, this includes the acquisition of materials, equipment. Uh, and that cost over the next five years is just over $113 million. Uh, and as mentioned earlier, we are also investing in our capital improvement program, our CIP, uh, to the tune of $100 million.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so the total five-year plan expenditure, uh, that this COSA, uh, will fund is $474 million.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so this shows the revenue increase over the next five years that are needed to be able to support that, uh, those planned expenditures, uh, again, starting with fifty-three percent in 2027, and then followed by smaller increases in the subsequent years. Uh, and that equates to a total compounded revenue of approximately a hundred and twenty percent over five years.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: A-a-and so, uh, moving on to, uh, the proposed rate structure, uh, it's comprised primarily of three components. Uh, number one is the variable water charge, right? This reflects how much water customers use, and this charge fluctuates, um, essentially based on your water usage. So the more water you use, the more you pay. We also have our fixed meter charge, and this supports the infrastructure that is required to maintain your meter, but essentially for being able to have access to the public water system.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, and again, this is based on your meter size. And then lastly, we have, uh, the pumping charge, uh, which reflects the energy that is required to deliver water to the higher elevation zones within our distribution system. And we do have a total of seven, uh, elevation zones, as you can see, zone one through zone seven there on the screen.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Um, and, and this table shows how customers are distributed across those elevation zones. Um, it bears mentioning that the majority of our customers, close to ninety percent, resides in those lower elevation zones, one through three. Uh, just over ten percent are in the higher elevation zones, uh, four through seven.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so in the next few slides, I will run through a few examples of how the proposed rates will impact typical customers. Uh, I do wanna preface that by saying, you know, every household is different, right? And, and so the actual bill impacts will vary. Uh, to that extent, we have created an online bill estimator tool and where, where you can put your actual, uh, water usage information.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: So you can input your meter size, your elevation zone, um, your consumption data, and it will give you a more customized estimate of what to expect, uh, within the next five years, so from years one, uh, through year five. And again, that tool is available online on our website, uh, glendale.gov prop- uh, forward slash proposed water rates.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Uh, or you can also contact us. Again, that contact information is referenced on the screen, and we're happy, uh, to provide that information to you. There is also a tutorial video online, um, which shows how to use this bill calculator, and that is also available in multiple languages.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: So with that being said, the first example we have is a single-family home with a three-quarter-inch meter in zone class one. And just to orient you here, the numbers at the top give you a sense of the monthly water use. And again, this is based on actual water use. And so for this particular example or this customer class, the median use is about ten HCF per month.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: Right. So that means half of these customers use t- uh, less than ten. The other half, they use more than ten. Uh, and just to back up and clarify, um, an HCF is-- stands for hundred cubic feet. Right. This is the standard unit by which we measure water use. Right. So one HCF is the equivalent of seven hundred and forty-eight gallons.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And so in this particular case, the average is twelve HCFs per month. And so that's twelve times seven hundred and forty-eight, which is, um, about eighty-nine hundred gallons per month. And so based on that usage, a typical single-family home using ten to twelve HCF per month would realize a monthly bill increase of approximately twenty-one dollars to twenty-six dollars.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: That is what is shown in the red box there, uh, near the bottom of the slide. And now you take the same single-family customer, the same usage, however, you now place them in elevation zone three, and now their monthly bill increase will be approximately twenty-nine dollars to about thirty-five and a half dollars.

transcript.speaker: speaker_3
transcript.text: And again, you take the same customer, however you place them at the highest elevation zone, uh, that is zone seven, and you can see their increase will be approximately seventy-one and a half dollars to about eighty-six dollars. es.overview: El Concejo Municipal de Glendale realizó una larga audiencia pública sobre un plan de Glendale Water & Power para subir las tarifas del agua durante cinco años, empezando con un aumento de ingresos del 53% el 1 de enero de 2027 y llegando a cerca del 120% en total para 2031. Decenas de residentes hablaron; la mayoría se opuso al aumento o pidió más tiempo. El concejo no tomó ninguna decisión sobre las tarifas. Votó 5–0 para mantener abierta la audiencia y volver a tratar el tema la próxima semana, así que hasta entonces todavía se pueden entregar protestas por escrito.

item-1.headline: El concejo pospone una semana la decisión sobre las tarifas del agua tras horas de testimonios, la mayoría en contra
item-1.summary: Glendale Water & Power (GWP) pidió al concejo aprobar cinco años de aumentos en las tarifas del agua: 53% más de ingresos en 2027 y luego 11%, 10%, 10% y 7%, lo que suma cerca del 120% en cinco años. El personal dijo que, desde 2018, los costos del agua importada, la electricidad y los equipos han subido mucho más rápido que las tarifas. El dinero se usaría para $100 millones en obras de tuberías, tanques, bombas, flujo de agua para incendios y medidores de agua, además de un bono de $40 millones que, según el personal, depende de que se empiece en enero. El personal dijo que una vivienda unifamiliar típica en la zona más baja pagaría entre $21 y $26 más al mes, y las viviendas en la zona más alta entre $71 y $86 más. Según la Proposición 218, una regla estatal que permite a los dueños de propiedades bloquear un aumento de tarifas con protestas por escrito, la secretaría informó que se recibieron 4,351 protestas, muy por debajo de las 22,738 necesarias. La mayoría de las personas que hablaron se opusieron al aumento o pidieron aplazarlo, mientras que unas pocas lo apoyaron. Los miembros del concejo mencionaron una carta tardía de Forest Lawn sobre las tarifas del agua reciclada y una idea del concejal Gharpetian de depender más de un cargo fijo por medidor. El personal dijo que necesitaba tiempo para estudiar esa idea y que requeriría un nuevo aviso público.
item-1.whyItMatters: Las tarifas del agua todavía no han cambiado, pero si el plan se aprueba la próxima semana, las facturas de agua de la mayoría de los clientes subirían mucho a partir del 1 de enero de 2027, y los residentes todavía pueden presentar protestas por escrito mientras la audiencia siga abierta.
item-1.result: Aprobado 5–0 mantener abierta la audiencia y continuar el tema una semana sin un nuevo aviso público
